title: A website after the first ten customers
metaTitle: The site after the first customers
excerpt: The early site won by speaking to the first users. The next one should help a sales call without burying the product those users already understood.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, a quieter room for a site that has to grow up.
caption: A room with one clear view through the arch. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should you replace the first marketing site?
faqs.answer: Replace it when sales calls keep explaining things the page should have said, or when the page still speaks only to the friends who found you early. Keep it when the offer is still true and the calls are only asking for one missing proof. A new visual system will not fix a sentence that no longer matches the product.

faqs.question: What should you add once real customers exist?
faqs.answer: Add the boundary of the offer, one or two customer situations told with permission, and a next step that matches how you actually sell. Show the product doing the job. Leave the origin story in a short paragraph unless it changes whether someone should talk to you.

faqs.question: How do you talk about early customers without overclaiming?
faqs.answer: Describe the situation and the job they hired the product to do, in words they would recognize. Skip logos you do not have permission to show, and skip numbers you would soften on a call. One accurate paragraph is stronger than a wall of implied scale.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A website after product market fit has a harder job than the page that found your first users. That early page could be specific, a little raw, and written for people who already felt the problem. The next one has to help a sales conversation without sanding off the product those people understood.

Keep the specificity. Add the pieces a buyer needs when another human will also be on the call: what is included, what happens after they start, and proof that is a situation rather than a mood.

## What the first site was allowed to be

The first site had one audience, often the audience you could name by first name. It could say "this is for teams who do X every Friday" and trust that the right ten people would feel seen. It could skip pricing shape, skip a security note, and skip the question of who implements the thing. Those people asked you directly.

That looseness was a feature. It let you learn the sentence. [Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has an intended audience and a primary purpose. The early page passed because the audience was narrow and the purpose was a conversation with them. The risk now is broadening the words until that purpose disappears.

Read the current homepage as if you were customer number eleven, with no intro from a friend. If the page still assumes a shared joke, it is time to write the joke out in full. If the page still describes a feature you removed in month three, the sales call is already starting with a correction. Corrections are how trust leaks before the demo begins.

Keep a copy of the old page. The sentences that early users quoted are evidence. You are editing them into a wider door, not throwing away the only language that has ever worked.

## The conversation the new page has to join

By the time you have a pipeline, the website is rarely the whole sale. Someone reads it before the call, during the call, and after, when they forward it to a colleague who was not there. The page has to support that second reader. They did not hear your aside. They have the URL and a minute.

[Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that they read only about a quarter of the words on pages they do open. The second reader will not finish your story. Put the offer, the product, and the way to talk in the part they will actually see. Put the longer proof where a careful person can open it, labeled, so the skim and the deep read are both honest.

Write the page so a colleague can sell from it when you are not in the room. That means the included work, the boundary, and the next step are visible. "We partner with ambitious teams" does not give them a sentence to forward. "We replace the Friday export with a view your ops lead can trust" does.

Ask the person who runs the calls which question they answer every time. That question is a missing section. If they always explain implementation, the page should show what the first week looks like. If they always explain who it is not for, write the boundary in public. The call should confirm the page, not reconstruct it.

## Keep the product in the frame

The failure mode of the second site is polish that forgets the product. A quiet marketing page, full of abstract benefit, sits in front of software that is specific and a little dense. The buyer feels the swap at login. They thought they were buying the calm page. They received the tool.

Show the product doing one job. A real screen, cropped so the job is visible, with a caption in the user's language. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public examples of product interfaces that can be read as interfaces. Your screenshot should work the same way. A visitor should be able to point at it and say what the person in the product is trying to finish.

If the product is still rough in places, show the path that is finished. Ten customers did not buy a mood. They bought a workflow. Hiding that workflow behind lifestyle imagery makes the site look earlier than the company is, which is a strange problem to create on purpose.

Match the words on the marketing page to the words in the product. If the app says "workspace" and the site says "hub," pick one. The second reader will try to find the word you used. When they cannot, they assume they are lost, or that the demo was a different product. Neither helps the call.

## Proof from the first ten, used with care

Early customers are the proof you actually have. Use them as situations, not as a logo farm. Describe the job they hired you for, the constraint, and what changed in their week. Get permission for the name. If you cannot name them, describe the role and the setting without pretending you have a famous list.

Skip the metrics you would qualify on the call. A precise number you cannot defend becomes the subject of the meeting. A sentence you can defend becomes a reason to take the meeting. You do not need a case-study industry. You need one true paragraph a skeptical buyer can repeat to their own team.

Place that paragraph next to the offer it supports. A story about onboarding belongs near the section on starting. A story about a weekly workflow belongs near the product shot of that workflow. A story dumped into a carousel at the bottom is easy to add and easy to miss, which means it will not help the second reader.

Do not let one friendly customer's language become the only language. They may have been unusually patient, or unusually similar to you. Check the paragraph against customer two and customer three. If it only flatters the first win, it will attract copies of that win and confuse everyone else.

## Pages that earn a place now

The early site could be one page. The sales-assisted site usually needs a few more, each with one job.

- A homepage that states the offer, shows the product, and routes the right person to a conversation.
- A page for the workflow you actually sell, with the boundary written down.
- Proof, even if it is two situations rather than a library.
- A plain answer to the question your calls keep repeating: security, implementation, pricing shape, or who it is for.

Pricing shape matters once people are choosing, even when the number is custom. Say what changes the price. Seats, usage, a setup period, a line you will not cross. Hiding the shape because the number varies forces every buyer to book a call just to learn they are in the wrong range. That call is a tax on both of you.

Keep the stack available to the technical reader without letting it lead. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Prisma, PostgreSQL, and Vercel are meaningful to someone who will inherit the product or integrate with it. They are not the reason a buyer starts. One short note, linked from the footer or the security section, is enough. The homepage still belongs to the job.

A docs entry or a changelog can start now, small. Ten customers will ask what changed. A public note in their language is kinder than an email only the founder remembers to send. Link it from the product, not only from a footer nobody opens after the contract.

## Language that should retire

Retire the sentences that were true for the first users and false for the next ones. "Built for our friends in the community" was warm when it was accurate. It sounds closed once you want a pipeline. "We do whatever you need" was flexible when you were learning. It sounds unbounded once a buyer is trying to scope a purchase.

Retire fake breadth. Adding three industries to the homepage because one customer in each existed will blur the offer that got you here. You can serve a second group when you can say the job in their words. Until then, the specific sentence is still the one that sells.

Retire urgency you do not mean. A banner about a closing cohort, a countdown, a "limited onboarding." If the truth is that you can start two teams this month, say that. A costume of scarcity trains buyers to discount the rest of the page.

Keep the voice that early users trusted. Plain, specific, a little careful. The second site fails when it hires a tone that could belong to any company that just raised. Your readers have already met the product. They will notice if the website starts speaking like a stranger.

## Edit the page, or replace it

Edit when the offer is still true and the structure is the problem. New proof, a clearer first sentence, the boundary written down, the product shot brought up. That is a revision. You can often do it on the site you have, especially if you own the repository and can change a headline without a project.

Replace the site when the story has actually changed. A different buyer. A product that no longer matches the screenshots. A homepage that cannot show the workflow without a rebuild of the layout. Say which of those you are looking at before you commission a new visual system. A new coat on the old sentence is how teams spend a quarter and recognize the same calls.

On a Hanabi project the useful question at this stage is practical. What must the next visitor understand, and what must the second reader be able to forward. The studio designs and builds, so the answer ends up in the page, not only in a deck. You should still leave with the repository and a place for the decisions, the client portal, where brand files and notes stay findable after the launch.

If the new page and the product start to feel like different companies, stop and fix that seam before you add more marketing. The walk-through of that problem is [when the marketing site and the product disagree](/blog/when-the-marketing-site-and-the-product-disagree). Read it before you polish a homepage that the app will contradict at login.

When you want a second pair of eyes on whether to edit or rebuild, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the page and the sentence your last three calls all had to repair. The half hour should tell you which repair belongs on the site.
